title: Federal Probes Expose Sprawling H-1B Visa Fraud Networks Across the U.S.
excerpt: From ghost offices in Texas to a $32 million racketeering conviction in Pennsylvania, a wave of federal and state investigations is targeting criminal enterprises that exploited the H-1B program for years.
body:
• Vice President JD Vance and the DOL Inspector General launched a broad investigation into H-1B and employment visa fraud in July 2026, issuing dozens of subpoenas targeting schemes worth "hundreds of millions" of dollars.
  • Pennsylvania brothers Bhaskar and Arun Savani were convicted in March 2026 of running a decade-long racketeering enterprise that included filing false H-1B applications and defrauding Medicaid of $32 million.
  • Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton opened investigations into three North Texas companies operating "ghost offices" to fraudulently sponsor H-1B visas.
  • DHS assessments have found as many as 21% of H-1B petitions to be fraudulent, raising scrutiny on all applicants — including legitimate Indian professionals.

A series of federal and state investigations has exposed the scale of criminal fraud within the H-1B visa program, with authorities uncovering schemes involving shell companies, fake offices, coerced wage kickbacks, and billions of dollars in related healthcare fraud.

The crackdowns span multiple agencies and jurisdictions, and while they target bad actors, immigration attorneys warn they are raising the bar for legitimate Indian H-1B applicants who already face intense scrutiny.

The Vance-DOL Probe

In July 2026, Vice President JD Vance and Department of Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito announced a sweeping investigation into foreigners exploiting worker visas. At an anti-fraud event in Milwaukee, Vance said labor officials had issued dozens of subpoenas to ensure "American jobs go to American workers and not foreign fraudsters."

D'Esposito told reporters the investigation had already "uncovered widespread schemes in which employers and labor brokers submitted fraudulent applications, exploited foreign workers through coercive wage-kickback arrangements, and undercut American workers by flooding the market with below-wage labor." He said the fraud extended to the medical industry, costing "hundreds of millions" of dollars, and was in some cases tied to cartels and transnational gangs.

The probe targets not only H-1B visa holders but also employment-based green card recipients. DHS assessments cited during the announcement found that as many as 21 percent of H-1B petitions were fraudulent.

"This is not just people working in factories or actual labor. These are people working in medical facilities and doctors' offices that are actually putting people in harm's way."

— Anthony D'Esposito, DOL Inspector General

The Savani Brothers: A Decade of Racketeering

In March 2026, a federal jury in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania convicted brothers Bhaskar and Arun Savani of running a criminal enterprise they called "the Savani Group." The operation, which spanned more than a decade, involved filing numerous false H-1B visa applications to bring foreign dental workers into the U.S., then forcing those workers into salary kickback arrangements.

The brothers used their fraudulently obtained workforce to run dental practices that billed Pennsylvania Medicaid over $32 million through nominee-owned clinics — even after their Medicaid contracts had been terminated. The scheme also involved obstructing a grand jury investigation, laundering proceeds through a complex web of transactions, wire fraud, and mail fraud.

Bhaskar Savani faces a statutory maximum of 420 years in prison. His brother faces up to 415 years. Sentencing hearings were scheduled for July 2026.

Ghost Offices in Texas

In January 2026, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton announced investigations into three North Texas companies suspected of setting up sham operations to fraudulently sponsor H-1B visas. Evidence showed at least one company registered a single-family home as its office and listed an empty, unfinished building as its worksite.

These companies had allegedly sponsored numerous H-1B visas despite no evidence they provided any of the products or services advertised on their websites. Paxton issued Civil Investigative Demands for employee records, financial statements, and internal communications.

"Any criminal who attempts to scam the H-1B visa program and use 'ghost offices' or other fraudulent ploys should be prepared to face the full force of the law."

— Ken Paxton, Texas Attorney General

What This Means for Legitimate H-1B Holders

For the hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals who hold or apply for H-1B visas through legitimate channels, these investigations create a more adversarial environment. USCIS has expanded its targeted site visits, focusing on companies where it cannot validate basic business information, H-1B-dependent employers with high ratios of visa workers, and situations where H-1B employees work off-site at client locations — a common arrangement in the Indian IT services industry.

Immigration attorneys advise legitimate H-1B holders and their employers to maintain thorough documentation of job duties, workplace locations, and wage compliance. Workers who suspect their employer is engaged in fraud can report tips to USCIS or file a complaint with the Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division.

The fraud investigations also feed into the broader political argument for restricting the H-1B program itself — a dynamic that concerns Indian tech workers who depend on the visa as their primary pathway to working in the United States.
nri_angle: Indian professionals are the largest group of H-1B holders, and expanded fraud investigations — including site visits targeting off-site workers common in Indian IT — raise the compliance bar for legitimate applicants.
author: Diaspora Desk
